arXiv:quant-ph/0004088v2 [quant-ph] 18 Jan 2026

Reversing quantum dynamics with near-optimal quantum and classical fidelity

Howard Barnum Affiliation: Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, NM 87545, USA Affiliation: Dept. of Computer Science, University of Bristol, Bristol BS8 1UB, UK    Emanuel Knill Affiliation: Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, NM 87545, USA
Abstract

We consider the problem of reversing quantum dynamics, with the goal of preserving an initial state’s quantum entanglement or classical correlation with a reference system. We exhibit an approximate reversal operation, adapted to the initial density operator and the “noise” dynamics to be reversed. We show that its error in preserving either quantum or classical information is no more than twice that of the optimal reversal operation. Applications to quantum algorithms and information transmission are discussed.

I Introduction

Counteracting the effects on quantum systems of noise generated by interaction with an environment is a central problem for the emerging field of quantum information processing. Its solution can be expected to have applications in quantum computation, precision measurement, and information transmission. In this paper we exhibit a reversal operation which takes account of both the noise and the initial density operator, to achieve near-optimal preservation of the initial density operator’s quantum entanglement or classical correlation with a reference system. We work throughout with finite-dimensional systems although we expect that the results generalize to infinite-dimensional ones, at least those with separable Hilbert spaces.

Section II reviews some of the theory of completely positive (CP) linear maps on spaces of operators on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. When these are trace-nonincreasing, they are also known in the quantum information/computation community as “quantum operations.” The only notation not standard in quantum information theory is our writing 𝒜∼{Ai}i\mathcal{A}\sim\{A_{i}\}_{i} to indicate that a CP-map acts as 𝒜⁡(ρ)=∑iAi​ρ​Ai†\mathcal{A}(\rho)=\sum_{i}A_{i}\rho A_{i}^{\dagger} . Section III reviews measures of fidelity commonly used in quantum information theory to quantify the effect of noise and information-processing operations on a system’s state, or an ensemble of system states. In addition, it motivates the particular measures we use, and indicates their connection to fidelity measures used in classical information-transmission theory. The measures we use concentrate on preserving the correlation or entanglement of a mixed state with a reference system. We explain why they are nevertheless relevant to the preservation of ensembles of pure states. This section includes several formal definitions required in the rest of the paper. Sections IV and VI are the core of the paper, containing the two main results. In Sec. IV the near-optimal reversal operation is defined, and we prove one of our main results: that the reversal operation’s error is no worse than twice that of the optimal reversal operation, for either quantum or classical information. Section V discusses the relationship of the reversal operation to a known near-optimal method of recovering classical information encoded in an ensemble of density operators, the “pretty good measurement”. When the noise can be viewed as encoding classical information in a completely decohered ensemble of density operators, our reversal operation can be viewed as performing the pretty-good measurement to distinguish these density operators. But when the noise operation may be viewed as encoding classical information into these density operators in a way which leaves some coherence between them, our reversal operation writes a nearly optimal estimate of the density operator into a set of orthogonal states without decohering these states as a measurement would. Section VI proves the other main result of the paper: a useful lower bound on the fidelity with which the reversal operation recovers classical information. This bound can be more tractable than the reversal operation’s fidelity itself, and has proven useful, for example, in discovering upper bounds on quantum query complexity. This and other applications are touched on in the concluding section.

II Quantum noise operations

We model quantum noise in a finite dimensional system QQ by the most general dynamics that can arise via a unitary interaction UQ​EU^{QE} with an environment EE initially independent of the system, in the sense that the initial joint density matrix of system and environment is a product ρQ⊗σE\rho^{Q}\otimes\sigma^{E}. The state of the system after the dynamics is obtained by tracing out the environment after UQ​EU^{QE} has been applied. We also model operations performed on a system in an attempt to counteract noise by such dynamics coupled to different, initially independent environment. For our purposes, where we ultimately care about the effect of operations on the system and perhaps on its entanglement with systems other than the environment, we may model operations with the environments starting in a pure state. This is because the effect on the system of a unitary interaction UQ​EU^{QE} with a mixed state σ\sigma of EE can be replicated by an interaction UQ​E1⊗IE2U^{QE_{1}}\otimes I^{E_{2}} with a pure state |0⟩\ket{0} of an environment E=E1⊗E2E=E_{1}\otimes E_{2} , whose partial trace onto E1E_{1} is equal to σ\sigma.

The most general dynamics thus obtained are trace-preserving completely positive maps 𝒜\mathcal{A} and can be represented in the form 𝒜:ρ↦∑iAi​ρ​Ai†\mathcal{A}:\rho\mapsto\sum_{i}A_{i}\rho A_{i}^{\dagger} for ρ\rho in the space of linear operators on QQ, where {Ai}i\{A_{i}\}_{i} is a finite family of linear operators on QQ. We normally leave the number of operators in the family unspecified. The condition that the dynamics is trace preserving implies that ∑iAi†​Ai=I\sum_{i}{A_{i}}^{\dagger}A_{i}=I. If the dynamics arises from tracing out the environment from the state UQ​E​(ρ⊗|0E⟩⟨0E|)​UQ​E†U^{QE}\quantity(\rho\otimes\ketbra{0^{E}}){U^{QE}}^{\dagger}, then

Ai=⟨iE|​UQ​E​|0E⟩\displaystyle A_{i}=\bra{i^{E}}U^{QE}\ket{0^{E}} (1)

are the “operator matrix elements” of the unitary interaction, with the elements computed between the environment initial state and states |iE⟩\ket{i^E} forming an orthonormal basis for the environment. In general we define the operator matrix element ⟨ξB|​OA​B​|ϕ⟩B\bra{\xi^{B}}O^{AB}\ket{\phi}^{B} of an operator OA​BO^{AB} as follows: Let the matrix elements of OO in some tensor product basis be Oi​j,i′​j′O_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}} and let ξj\xi_{j} and ϕj\phi_{j} be the components of |ξ⟩\ket{\xi} and |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} in the basis |jB⟩\ket{j^{B}}. Then the operator matrix element ⟨ξB|​OA​B​|ϕ⟩B\bra{\xi^{B}}O^{AB}\ket{\phi}^{B} is the operator XX on AA whose matrix elements in the basis |iA⟩\ket{i^{A}} are given by

⟨i|​X​|i′⟩=∑j,j′ξj∗​ϕj′​Oi​j,i′​j′.\displaystyle\bra{i}X\ket{i'}=\sum_{j,j^{\prime}}\xi^{*}_{j}\phi_{j^{\prime}}O_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}. (2)

States Ai​|ψ⟩A_{i}\ket{\psi} obtained by applying AiA_{i} to an initial state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} of QQ are often called the (unnormalized) “relative state” of the system QQ, in the sense that it is relative to the environment basis state |iE⟩\ket{i^{E}} after the unitary interaction. The overall evolution of system and environment is

|ψQ⟩​|0E⟩→UQ​E​|ψQ⟩​|0E⟩=∑iAiQ​|ψQ⟩​|iE⟩\displaystyle\ket{\psi^{Q}}\ket{0^{E}}\rightarrow U^{QE}\ket{\psi^{Q}}\ket{0^{E}}=\sum_{i}A_{i}^{Q}\ket{\psi^{Q}}\ket{i^{E}} (3)

That the state on the right-hand side is normalized for normalized input states is equivalent to the requirement that ∑iAi†​Ai=I\sum_{i}{A_{i}}^{\dagger}A_{i}=I for trace-preserving quantum operations. Quantum operations in general are trace-nonincreasing, which is equivalent to the requirement that ∑iAi†​Ai≤I\sum_{i}{A_{i}}^{\dagger}A_{i}\leq I. Quantum operations 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfy that if F≤GF\leq G are positive semidefinite operators, than 𝒜⁡(F)≤𝒜⁡(G)\mathcal{A}(F)\leq\mathcal{A}(G).

If the environment is considered as a measuring apparatus with the states of the basis |iE⟩\ket{i^{E}} its “pointer variables” [1] corresponding to different measurement results, then Ai​|ψ⟩A_{i}\ket{\psi} is the state of the system conditional on the apparatus measurement outcome ii after coupling. The squared norm of Ai​|ψ⟩A_{i}\ket{\psi} is the probability of the measurement outcome ii. The overall operation 𝒜\mathcal{A} represents the dynamics of the measurement averaged over measurement results, corresponding to the sitatuation where the measurement results are ignored. Of course, a trace-preserving operation need not arise from an actual ignored measurement in this manner, but it may always be viewed this way, in terms of averaging over a notional readout of the environment in some “pointer basis”, if desired.

The 𝒜i\mathcal{A}_{i} are said to form a decomposition of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, for which we use the notation 𝒜∼{Ai}i\mathcal{A}\sim\{A_{i}\}_{i}. Using a different orthonormal “pointer basis” [1] for the environment in Eq. (1) results in a different decomposition of the same operation. Two such pointer bases are related by a unitary transformation of the environment. The corresponding decompositions of the operation are related by the unitary VV that takes the pointer basis used to define the AjA_{j} to that used to define the BiB_{i}:

Bi=∑jVj​i∗​Aj,\displaystyle B_{i}=\sum_{j}{V_{ji}}^{*}A_{j}, (4)

where Vj​i=⟨jE|​V​|iE⟩V_{ji}=\bra{j^{E}}V\ket{i^{E}} are the entries of VV in the pointer basis |iE⟩\ket{i^{E}} used to define the AjA_{j}.

III Quantifying the effects of noise

Let us consider how to quantify the effects of a noise operation on information contained in a quantum system, using the classical Shannon theory of information transmission as a guide. The information we have about a set of classical alternatives indexed by ii of a local system TT is usually measured by the entropy of the probabilities we ascribe to the alternatives: H(𝒑)≔−∑ipilog⁡(pi)H(\bm{p})\coloneqq-\sum_{i}p_{i}\log(p_{i}). Suppose we want to be able to transmit or store the classical states ii, which will be presented to us with the probabilities pip_{i} . We encode them on a system TT, while keeping a reference copy with us, on a system RR. In transmission, TT is then affected by noise. We might define perfect success as the preservation of the initial perfect correlation between RR and TT. In terms of the probability measures, we want the initial and final joint mixed states of reference RR and system TT both to be described by p⁡(iR,jT)=pi​δiR​jTp(i^{R},j^{T})=p_{i}\delta_{i^{R}j^{T}}. If our actual, noise-affected transmission results in the mixed state with joint probability distribution q⁡(iR,jT)q(i^{R},j^{T}), we could measure how well we have succeeded by looking at the distance between p⁡(iR,jT)p(i^{R},j^{T}) and q⁡(iR,jT)q(i^{R},j^{T}) using some standard measure of distance between probability distributions. To give examples of such distances, let 𝒓=(r1,…,rn),𝒔=(s1,…,sn)\bm{r}=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{n}),\bm{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}) be probabilities on a common set of classical alternatives labeled 1,…,n1,\ldots,n. We can, for example, measure the distance between rr and ss by the classical infidelity B⁡(𝒓,𝒔)≔1−(∑krk1/2​sk1/2)2B(\bm{r},\bm{s})\coloneqq 1-\quantity(\sum_{k}r_{k}^{1/2}s_{k}^{1/2})^{2}, which is a function of the Bhattacharyya coefficient. The total variation distance 12​∑i​j|rk−sk|\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij}|r_{k}-s_{k}| is another reasonable choice. We assume that q⁡(i,j)=pi​t​(j|i)q(i,j)=p_{i}t(j|i), where t⁡(j|i)t(j|i) is a stochastic matrix of transition probabilities describing the noise. Using the classical infidelity to measure how well the original correlation has been preserved in the above-given example gives

1−(∑i,jδi​j​pi1/2​q​(i,j)1/2)2=1−(∑ipi1/2​q​(i,i)1/2)2=1−(∑ipi​t​(i|i)1/2)2.\displaystyle 1-\quantity(\sum_{i,j}\delta_{ij}p_{i}^{1/2}q(i,j)^{1/2})^{2}=1-\quantity(\sum_{i}p_{i}^{1/2}q(i,i)^{1/2})^{2}=1-\quantity(\sum_{i}p_{i}t(i|i)^{1/2})^{2}. (5)

Using the total variation distance gives

12​∑i​j|δi​j​pi−pi​t​(j|i)|\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij}|\delta_{ij}p_{i}-p_{i}t(j|i)| =∑i​j:pi​t​(j|i)>pipit(j|i)−δi​jpi\displaystyle=\sum_{ij:p_{i}t(j|i)>p_{i}}p_{i}t(j|i)-\delta_{ij}p_{i}
=∑i​j:j≠ipit(j|i)\displaystyle=\sum_{ij:j\neq i}p_{i}t(j|i)
=∑ipi​∑j≠it⁡(j|i).\displaystyle=\sum_{i}p_{i}\sum_{j\neq i}t(j|i). (6)

The expression ∑j≠it⁡(j|i)\sum_{j\neq i}t(j|i) is the probability that, if ii is sent, a different message is received. The total variation distance therefore is the same as the familiar “error probability” criterion for channel transmission: the average, over messages ii, of the probability that ii is sent but a different message is received. This can be interpreted as an average pure-state infidelity where the reference pure state for input ii is |i⟩\ket{i}, but we have shown that it can be rewritten as a distance from a mixed state representing perfect initial correlation. For information theoretic purposes, the classical infidelity and the total variation distance have closely related behaviors. The relationships can be determined from the inequalities given in Ref. [2], Prop. 5.

We have gone through this analysis to indicate that there is a classical analog of the approach we here take to quantum as well as classical fidelity: investigating the effects of noise on a channel, which we may want to use to transmit pure states, by looking at its effect on a state whose marginal distribution on the noise-affected system is a mixed state corresponding to the ensemble of possible pure-state messages. Thus an approach which might be viewed as unnecessarily concerned with the fidelity of mixed states, provides a good fidelity criterion for the problem of transmitting pure states which are supplied to the channel with probabilities pip_{i}, where the fidelity criterion is in terms of the idea of preservation of correlation with a possibly notional reference system.

We now apply the classical analysis given above to the problem of transmitting quantum information, specifically the problem of evaluating the fidelity with which a given operation preserves quantum information. We resume consideration of the noise operation 𝒜\mathcal{A}, which is the analog of the classical stochastic channel matrix t⁡(i|j)t(i|j) presented earlier. For the purpose of defining entanglement fidelities, we weaken the trace-preserving property and consider general quantum operations, namely trace-nonincreasing, completely positive maps 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Now, rather than preservation of the noise-affected system’s correlation with a reference system, we require preservation of its entanglement. Just as the classical reference system could be completely notional, the quantum reference system may also be taken to be completely notional. In both cases, the reference system is introduced because high-fidelity preservation of correlation with the reference system implies high-fidelity preservation of states on the noise-affected system when they are supplied to the channel with the marginal distribution pip_{i}. When 𝒜\mathcal{A} acts on QQ, a state |ψ0R​Q⟩≔∑ipi​|iR⟩​|iQ⟩\ket{\psi_{0}^{RQ}}\coloneqq\sum_{i}\sqrt{p_{i}}\ket{i^{R}}\ket{i^{Q}} entangled with a reference system RR evolves as

|Ψ0⟩≔∑ipi​|iR⟩​|iQ⟩​|0E⟩→|Ψf⟩≔∑i​jpi​|iR⟩​Aj​|iQ⟩​|jE⟩.\displaystyle\ket{\Psi_{0}}\coloneqq\sum_{i}\sqrt{p_{i}}\ket{i^{R}}\ket{i^{Q}}\ket{0^{E}}\rightarrow\ket{\Psi_{f}}\coloneqq\sum_{ij}\sqrt{p_{i}}\ket{i^{R}}A_{j}\ket{i^{Q}}\ket{j^{E}}. (7)

The entanglement fidelity Fe​(ρ,𝒜)F_{e}(\rho,\mathcal{A}) is defined as ‖P0​|Ψf⟩‖2\|P_{0}\ket{\Psi_{f}}\|^{2}, where P0≔|ψ0R​Q⟩​⟨ψ0R​Q|⊗IEP_{0}\coloneqq\ket{\psi_{0}^{RQ}}\bra{\psi_{0}^{RQ}}\otimes I^{E} [3]. Thus FeF_{e} is the squared norm of the projection of the final state in Eq. (7) onto the subspace associated with the initial entangled state |ψ0R​Q⟩\ket{\psi_{0}^{RQ}}. It depends only on ρ≔∑ipi​|iQ⟩​⟨iQ|\rho\coloneqq\sum_{i}p_{i}\ket{i^{Q}}\bra{i^{Q}}, and satisfies

Fe​(ρ,𝒜)=∑i|tr⁡Ai​ρ|2.\displaystyle F_{e}(\rho,\mathcal{A})=\sum_{i}|\tr A_{i}\rho|^{2}. (8)

We can also define the input-output fidelity for a pure state |ψ⟩⟨ψ|\outerproduct{\psi}{\psi} as F⁡(|ψ⟩,𝒜)=⟨ψ|​𝒜​(|ψ⟩⟨ψ|)​|ψ⟩F(\ket{\psi},\mathcal{A})=\bra{\psi}\mathcal{A}(\outerproduct{\psi}{\psi})\ket{\psi}, which is the fidelity of the final state of QQ onto its initial state. As in the classical case with correlation, using entanglement for the quantum case does not reflect a fixation on entanglement, but also provides an appropriate fidelity criterion even when it is preservation of pure states on the system QQ that we are concerned with, and no entangled system RR in fact exists. This is because the entanglement fidelity Fe​(ρQ,𝒜)F_{e}(\rho^{Q},\mathcal{A}) is a lower bound on the average input–output fidelity ∑iqi​F​(|ψi⟩,𝒜)\sum_{i}q_{i}F(\ket{\psi_{i}},\mathcal{A}) for any pure-state ensemble on QQ consisting of |ψi⟩\ket{\psi_{i}} with probability qiq_{i} for which its density operator σQ=∑iqi​|ψi⟩⟨ψi|\sigma^{Q}=\sum_{i}q_{i}\outerproduct{\psi_{i}}{\psi_{i}} satisfies σQ=ρQ\sigma^{Q}=\rho^{Q}. While this is a good lower bound on the input–output fidelities of pure-state ensembles, it is not in general a tight lower bound on the input–output fidelity. Thus if one is really interested only in the effect of a quantum channel on a particular ensemble, one might get fidelities much higher than the entanglement fidelity suggests. We will be interested in one such case, the input–output fidelity for an orthonormal set of states, related to the ability to preserve essentially classical information coded in a quantum channel. In order to treat this case by utilizing entanglement fidelities, we introduce a notion which generalizes both: average entanglement fidelity.

For an ensemble E={pi,ρi}iE=\{p_{i},\rho_{i}\}_{i} where state ρi\rho_{i} occurs with probability pip_{i}, we define the average entanglement fidelity by

F¯e​(E,𝒜)≔∑ipi​Fe​(ρi,𝒜).\displaystyle\bar{F}_{e}(E,\mathcal{A})\coloneqq\sum_{i}p_{i}F_{e}(\rho_{i},\mathcal{A}). (9)

A special case is

Fcl​(ρ,𝒜)≔∑ipi​⟨i|​𝒜​(|i⟩⟨i|)​|i⟩=F¯e​({pi,|i⟩⟨i|}i,𝒜),\displaystyle F_{\text{cl}}(\rho,\mathcal{A})\coloneqq\sum_{i}p_{i}\bra{i}\mathcal{A}(\outerproduct{i}{i})\ket{i}=\bar{F}_{e}(\{p_{i},\outerproduct{i}{i}\}_{i},\mathcal{A}), (10)

where the |i⟩\ket{i} form an eigenbasis of ρ\rho with ρ=∑ipi​|i⟩⟨i|\rho=\sum_{i}p_{i}\outerproduct{i}{i}. This is the classical fidelity for the classical information of the ensemble of orthogonal eigenstates of the input density operator ρ\rho. Another special case is an ensemble consisting of a single density operator ρ\rho. In this case F¯e\bar{F}_{e} is just Fe​(ρ,𝒜)F_{e}(\rho,\mathcal{A}).

The average entanglement fidelity can equivalently be expressed as the norm squared of the projection of the overall final state onto the subspace in which entangled states |ψiR​Q⟩\ket{\psi_{i}^{RQ}} representing the initial ensemble are correctly correlated with orthogonal states of an additional reference system SS. There are different choices of states of R​Q​SRQS that have such correct correlations. One is |ψ0R​Q​S⟩=∑ipi​|ψiR​Q⟩​|iS⟩\ket{\psi_{0}^{RQS}}=\sum_{i}\sqrt{p_{i}}\ket{\psi_{i}^{RQ}}\ket{i^{S}}, which represents the correlation by entanglement with SS. Another is the mixed state |ψ0R​Q​S⟩⟨ψ0R​Q​S|=∑ipi​|ψiR​Q⟩⟨ψiR​Q|⊗|iS⟩⟨iS|\outerproduct{\psi_{0}^{RQS}}{\psi_{0}^{RQS}}=\sum_{i}p_{i}\outerproduct{\psi_{i}^{RQ}}{\psi_{i}^{RQ}}\otimes\outerproduct{i^{S}}{i^{S}}, for which the correlation is classical. With either choice, an equivalent expression for average entanglement fidelity is

F¯e\displaystyle\bar{F}_{e} =‖Pc⊗IE​|Ψf⟩‖2\displaystyle=\|P_{c}\otimes I^{E}\ket{\Psi_{f}}\|^{2}
=tr⁡Pc​ℐR​S⊗𝒜​(|ψ0R​Q​S⟩⟨ψ0R​Q​S|),\displaystyle=\tr P_{c}\mathcal{I}^{RS}\otimes\mathcal{A}\quantity(\ketbra{\psi_{0}^{RQS}}), (11)

where Pc≔∑i|is⟩⟨is|⊗|ψiR​Q⟩⟨ψiR​Q|P_{c}\coloneqq\sum_{i}\outerproduct{i^{s}}{i^{s}}\otimes\outerproduct{\psi_{i}^{RQ}}{\psi_{i}^{RQ}}. This expression does not depend on whether the correlation with SS in |ψ0R​Q​S⟩⟨ψ0R​Q​S|\outerproduct{\psi_{0}^{RQS}}{\psi_{0}^{RQS}} is obtained by entanglement or merely classically.

For example, consider the special case of Fcl​(ρ,𝒜)F_{\text{cl}}(\rho,\mathcal{A}) . Here the reference system RR plays no role as the ρi\rho_{i} are pure. After suppressing RR, Pc=∑i|iS⟩​|iQ⟩​⟨iQ|​⟨iS|P_{c}=\sum_{i}\ket{i^{S}}\ket{i^{Q}}\bra{i^{Q}}\bra{i^{S}}. SS contains a record of the classical information sent. SS and QQ may be supposed to be either entangled or classically correlated, with ρ0S​Q=∑i,jpi​pj​|iS⟩⟨jS|⊗|iQ⟩⟨jQ|\rho_{0}^{SQ}=\sum_{i,j}\sqrt{p_{i}p_{j}}\outerproduct{i^{S}}{j^{S}}\otimes\outerproduct{i^{Q}}{j^{Q}} or ρ0S​Q=∑ipi​|iS⟩⟨iS|⊗|iQ⟩⟨iQ|\rho_{0}^{SQ}=\sum_{i}p_{i}\outerproduct{i^{S}}{i^{S}}\otimes\outerproduct{i^{Q}}{i^{Q}}, for orthonormal system and reference bases |i⟩\ket{i}, where the system basis is the eigenbasis of ρ\rho. In either case, computing the probability tr⁡(Pc​ρfS​Q)\tr(P_{c}\rho_{f}^{SQ}) that the final system-reference state falls into the subspace in which system and reference exhibit perfect classical correlation in the desired bases, gives the classical fidelity Fcl​(ρ,𝒜)F_{\text{cl}}(\rho,\mathcal{A}).

IV The reversal operation

We motivate the definition of the near-optimal reversal operation ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} by considering operations 𝒜\mathcal{A} that are perfectly reversible on a “code” subspace CC. Let PCP_{C} be the projector onto CC. Perfectly reversible operations have a decomposition AiA_{i} for which Ai​PC=pi​WiA_{i}P_{C}=\sqrt{p_{i}}W_{i} for some probabilities pip_{i}, where the WiW_{i} are isometries from CC into orthogonal subspaces, which means that Wi†​Wj=δi​j​PCW_{i}^{\dagger}W_{j}=\delta_{ij}P_{C} [4, 5]. Intuitively, this means that as far as its action on the code subspace is concerned, the operation just maps the state isometrically into one of a set of mutually orthogonal subspaces. Without loss of generality, assume that the ranges of the WiW_{i} together span the state space. The reversal operation has a decomposition consisting of the operators Wi†=PC​Ai†/piW_{i}^{\dagger}=P_{C}A_{i}^{\dagger}/\sqrt{p_{i}}. Intuitively, it may be thought of as measurement of which of the subspaces the state was mapped isometrically to, followed by the inverse of that isometry to put it correctly back into the code space. This resembles the adjoint of the restriction 𝒜C\mathcal{A}_{C} of 𝒜\mathcal{A} to CC with respect to the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product (A,B)=tr⁡A†​B(A,B)=\tr A^{\dagger}B, which is given by 𝒜C†∼{PC​Ai†}i\mathcal{A}_{C}^{\dagger}\sim\{P_{C}A_{i}^{\dagger}\}_{i}. To get the reversal operation, the pi\sqrt{p_{i}} need to be cancelled, which also makes the operation trace preserving. The general definition of the reversal operation ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} is also based on the adjoint, suitably corrected to ensure that it is trace preserving. The reversal operation is defined as

ℛ𝒜,ρ∼{ρ1/2Ai†𝒜(ρ)−1/2}i,\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho}\sim\{\rho^{1/2}A_{i}^{\dagger}\mathcal{A}(\rho)^{-1/2}\}_{i}\;, (12)

where we assume that 𝒜⁡(ρ)\mathcal{A}(\rho) has full support. In our analyses, the orthogonal complement of the support of 𝒜⁡(ρ)\mathcal{A}(\rho) contributes nothing, so there is no loss of generality in making this assumption. If we apply this definition to an operation 𝒜\mathcal{A} that is perfectly reversible on a code, using as our input ρ\rho any state with support the code, it can be verified that this definition matches the reversal operation for codes described previously.

The notation ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} does not refer to a specific decomposition of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, which is justified by:

Lemma 1.

The definition of the reversal operation ℛ⁡(𝒜,ρ)\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{A},\rho) is independent of the decomposition {Ai}i\{A_{i}\}_{i} of 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

Proof.

Proof: Let 𝒜∼{Bi}i\mathcal{A}\sim\{B_{i}\}_{i} be another decomposition. By adding null operators to one of the two decompositions, we can ensure that both have the same number of operators. Adding null operators to {Ai}i\{A_{i}\}_{i} does not change the action of ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho}. Then there exist Ui​jU_{ij} such that Bi=∑jUi​j​AjB_{i}=\sum_{j}U_{ij}A_{j}, where the matrix UU with entries Ui​jU_{ij} is unitary. The decomposition of ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} in terms of the Ai†A_{i}^{\dagger} given in Eq. (12) transforms via the coefficients of the entry-wise complex conjugate U∗U^{*} of UU into a decomposition given in terms of the Bi†B_{i}^{\dagger}. As U∗U^{*} is also unitary, the result is another decomposition of the same operation. ∎

A simple but important property of ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} can be verified directly from the definition:

Proposition 2.

ℛ𝒜,ρ​(𝒜​(ρ))=ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho}(\mathcal{A}(\rho))=\rho.

The operation ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} is near-optimal in the sense given by the following theorem.

Theorem 3.

Let E={pi,ρi}iE=\{p_{i},\rho_{i}\}_{i} be an ensemble of commuting density matrices. Let ρ=∑ipi​ρi\rho=\sum_{i}p_{i}\rho_{i}. Then for every trace-preserving, completely positive map ℛ\mathcal{R},

F¯e​(E,ℛ𝒜,ρ​𝒜)≥F¯e​(E,ℛ​𝒜)2.\displaystyle\bar{F}_{e}(E,\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho}\mathcal{A})\geq\bar{F}_{e}(E,\mathcal{R}\mathcal{A})^{2}. (13)

As a corollary, if F¯e​(E,ℛ​𝒜)=1−η\bar{F}_{e}(E,\mathcal{R}\mathcal{A})=1-\eta, then F¯e​(E,ℛ𝒜,ρ​𝒜)≥(1−η)2≥1−2​η\bar{F}_{e}(E,\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho}\mathcal{A})\geq(1-\eta)^{2}\geq 1-2\eta. That is, the error of ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho}, defined as one minus the entanglement fidelity, is never greater than twice that of the best reversal operation.

Two important special cases of Thm. 3 are in the following corollary.

Corollary 4.

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} be a trace-preserving completely positive map. Then Fcl​(ρ,ℛ​𝒜)≤Fcl​(ρ,ℛ𝒜,ρ​𝒜)F_{\rm cl}(\rho,\mathcal{R}\mathcal{A})\leq\sqrt{F_{\rm cl}(\rho,\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho}\mathcal{A})} and Fe​(ρ,ℛ​𝒜)≤Fe​(ρ,ℛ𝒜,ρ​𝒜)F_{e}(\rho,\mathcal{R}\mathcal{A})\leq\sqrt{F_{e}(\rho,\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho}\mathcal{A})}.

When the members of the input ensemble ρi\rho_{i} do not commute, we do not know whether ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} for ρ=∑ipi​ρi\rho=\sum_{i}p_{i}\rho_{i} is still near-optimal.

V Relationship to the “pretty good measurement”

The above-presented analysis of the fidelity of reversal makes it clear that ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} provides a method for distinguishing, with close to optimal average error, density matrices from the ensemble {pj,ρ^j}j\{p_{j},\hat{\rho}_{j}\}_{j}, where ρ^j≔𝒜⁡(|j⟩⟨j|)\hat{\rho}_{j}\coloneqq\mathcal{A}(\outerproduct{j}{j}) and ρ=∑jpj​|j⟩⟨j|\rho=\sum_{j}p_{j}\outerproduct{j}{j}. This provides a near-optimal method for distinguishing density matrices in an arbitrary ensemble, since any ensemble {pj,ρ^j}j\{p_{j},\hat{\rho}_{j}\}_{j} may be constructed by an operation

𝒜∼{λi​j​|vi​j⟩⟨j|}i​j,\displaystyle\mathcal{A}\sim\{\sqrt{\lambda_{ij}}\outerproduct{v_{ij}}{j}\}_{ij}, (35)

where ρ^j=∑iλi​j​|vi​j⟩⟨vi​j|\hat{\rho}_{j}=\sum_{i}\lambda_{ij}\outerproduct{v_{ij}}{v_{ij}} are the spectral decompositions of the density matrices to be distinguished. The operation 𝒜\mathcal{A} may be thought of as measuring in the orthogonal basis |j⟩\ket{j}, and then producing the corresponding ρ^j\hat{\rho}_{j}, for example, by randomly applying with probabilities λi​j\lambda_{ij} unitary rotations taking |j⟩\ket{j} to |vi​j⟩\ket{v_{ij}}. With this operation 𝒜\mathcal{A},

ℛ𝒜,ρ∼{Ri​j}i​j={pjλi​j|j⟩⟨vi​j|ρout−1/2}i​j,\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho}\sim\{R_{ij}\}_{ij}=\quantity{\sqrt{p_{j}}\sqrt{\lambda_{ij}}\ketbra{j}{v_{ij}}\rho_{\text{out}}^{-1/2}}_{ij}, (36)

where ρout=∑jpj​ρ^j\rho_{\text{out}}=\sum_{j}p_{j}\hat{\rho}_{j}. The “pretty good measurement” (PGM) was introduced by Holevo [7] for the case of linearly independent pure states, in which case the PGM is a measurement of orthogonal projectors, and as Holevo showed, the optimal such measurement. The term “pretty good measurement” is from Ref. [8]. For an ensemble of unnormalized density matrices ρj≔pj​ρ^j\rho_{j}\coloneqq p_{j}\hat{\rho}_{j} so that ρout=∑jρj\rho_{\text{out}}=\sum_{j}\rho_{j} is a normalized density operator, the PGM is defined by the set of operators consisting of the

Xj≔ρout−1/2ρjρout−1/2.\displaystyle X_{j}\coloneqq\rho_{\text{out}}^{-1/2}\rho_{j}\rho_{\text{out}}^{-1/2}. (37)

For pure states ρj\rho_{j} with ρj∝|vj⟩⟨vj|\rho_{j}\propto\outerproduct{v_{j}}{v_{j}}, these are just the operators corresponding to the “ρ\rho-distorted” [9] states ρout−1/2|vj⟩\rho_{\text{out}}^{-1/2}\ket{v_{j}}. Note that for a doubly indexed ensemble consisting of unnormalized states ρi​j\rho_{ij} with ∑iρi​j=ρj\sum_{i}\rho_{ij}=\rho_{j}, we have ∑iXi​j=Xj\sum_{i}X_{ij}=X_{j}, where the XjX_{j} are the PGM for the ensemble consisting the ρj\rho_{j}. The operation in Eq. (36) may be viewed, via the given representation, as performing the PGM for the ensemble consisting of the unnormalized states pj​λi​j​|vi​j⟩\sqrt{p_{j}}\sqrt{\lambda_{ij}}\ket{v_{ij}}, and returning |j⟩\ket{j} when the measurement result i,ji,j is obtained. Indeed, for this ensemble Ri​j†​Ri​j=Xi​j{R_{ij}}^{\dagger}R_{ij}=X_{ij}, and therefore ∑iRi​j†​Ri​j=Xj\sum_{i}{R_{ij}}^{\dagger}R_{ij}=X_{j}. Thus the operation may also be viewed as doing the PGM for the ρj\rho_{j}, and returning |j⟩\ket{j} when the measurement result is jj . Since the |j⟩\ket{j} are orthogonal, this is “classical information”: the label jj is viewed as the estimate of which jj was input. However, a given ensemble consisting of the ρj\rho_{j} may in general arise from orthogonal states |j⟩\ket{j} by actions of channels different from the “classicizing” one of Eq (35), which completely decoheres the orthogonal states |j⟩\ket{j} before producing ρ^j\hat{\rho}_{j}. For example, if the ρ^j\hat{\rho}_{j} are orthogonal and pure they may be produced either by measurement in the basis |j⟩\ket{j} followed by an appropriate unitary operator UU, or by applying UU without prior measurement. In the first case quantum coherence is completely destroyed, while in the second case it is perfectly preserved. When the channel producing the ρ^j\hat{\rho}_{j} is not of the form in Eq. (35), the reversal operation ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} will be different from the one in Eq. (36). Although the operation of Eq. (36) still gives near-optimal classical fidelity, it will not necessarily give good entanglement fidelity, since in some sense it decoheres the states ρ^j\hat{\rho}_{j} . ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho}, however, has near-optimal entanglement fidelity while retaining near-optimal classical fidelity. ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} thus takes advantage of whatever coherence remains between the ρ^j\hat{\rho}_{j}; it avoids decohering the ρ^j\hat{\rho}_{j} if the channel has not decohered them already.

VI A bound on the classical fidelity of reversal

To bound a fidelity of reversal it is sufficient to bound the fidelity for the near optimal reversal operation and apply Thm. 3. Here we have a look at such bounds for classical fidelities of reversal for 𝒜\mathcal{A} of the form in Eq. (35). In this case, the classical fidelities are average probabilities of success for measurements that attempt to infer which of the eigenprojectors |j⟩⟨j|\outerproduct{j}{j} of the input state ρ=∑jpj​|j⟩⟨j|\rho=\sum_{j}p_{j}\outerproduct{j}{j} was actually transmitted. The expression for the PGM gives the following bound on the optimal probability of success FclF_{\text{cl}}, with the definitions of Sec. V.

Fcl2\displaystyle F_{\text{cl}}^{2} ≥Fcl​(ρ,ℛ𝒜,ρ​𝒜)\displaystyle\geq F_{\text{cl}}(\rho,\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho}\mathcal{A})
=∑jtrρout−1/2ρjρout−1/2ρj\displaystyle=\sum_{j}\tr\rho_{\text{out}}^{-1/2}\rho_{j}\rho_{\text{out}}^{-1/2}\rho_{j}
=1−∑i,j:i≠jtrρout−1/2ρiρout−1/2ρj,\displaystyle=1-\sum_{i,j:i\neq j}\tr\rho_{\text{out}}^{-1/2}\rho_{i}\rho_{\text{out}}^{-1/2}\rho_{j}, (38)

where we used the identity ∑i,jtrρout−1/2ρiρout−1/2ρj=1\sum_{i,j}\tr\rho_{\text{out}}^{-1/2}\rho_{i}\rho_{\text{out}}^{-1/2}\rho_{j}=1. Thus the probability of error EclE_{\text{cl}} is bounded above by 2∑i,j:i≠jtrρout−1/2ρiρout−1/2ρj2\sum_{i,j:i\neq j}\tr\rho_{\text{out}}^{-1/2}\rho_{i}\rho_{\text{out}}^{-1/2}\rho_{j}, which is a multiple of the sum of the Hilbert–Schmidt inner products of the different ρout−1/4ρjρout−1/4\rho_{\text{out}}^{-1/4}\rho_{j}\rho_{\text{out}}^{-1/4}. When ρout\rho_{\text{out}} is proportional to a projection, this sum can be easy to estimate. An often used measure of overlap between density matrices is the Bures–Uhlmann fidelity [10, 11]. This measure depends only on the pair of density matrices, and is defined by FBU​(σ1,σ2)≔tr⁡σ11/2​σ2​σ11/2F_{\text{BU}}(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2})\coloneqq\tr\sqrt{\sigma_{1}^{1/2}\sigma_{2}\sigma_{1}^{1/2}}. The expression for the optimal reversal given in Eq. (36) can be used to derive a bound on the probability of error in terms of the Bures–Uhlmann fidelities.

Fcl2≥1−∑i,j:i≠jpi​pjFBU(ρ^i,ρ^j).\displaystyle F_{\rm cl}^{2}\geq 1-\sum_{i,j:i\neq j}\sqrt{p_{i}p_{j}}F_{\rm BU}(\hat{\rho}_{i},\hat{\rho}_{j}). (39)

Since |R​A|22|RA|_{2}^{2} is one, it suffices to estimate the sum of the squared Frobenius norms of the off-diagonal blocks of R​ARA to bound the optimal FclF_{\text{cl}}. To do so, let B=(R​A)†​(R​A)=(R​A)2=A†​AB=(RA)^{\dagger}(RA)=(RA)^{2}=A^{\dagger}A. The squared Frobenius norm of the off-diagonal block at block position k,lk,l of R​ARA is the trace of the block Bk​l=Ak†​AlB_{kl}={A_{k}}^{\dagger}A_{l} at block position k,lk,l of BB. Since Ak​Ak†=ρkA_{k}{A_{k}}^{\dagger}=\rho_{k} and by polar decomposition of AlA_{l},

Bk​l†​Bk​l=Al†​ρk​Al=U​ρl1/2​ρk​ρl1/2​U†\displaystyle{B_{kl}}^{\dagger}B_{kl}={A_{l}}^{\dagger}\rho_{k}A_{l}=U\rho_{l}^{1/2}\rho_{k}\rho_{l}^{1/2}U^{\dagger} (42)

for some unitary operator UU depending on ll. Consequently, the L1L_{1}-norm of Bk​lB_{kl}, defined by |Bk​l|1=tr⁡Bk​l†​Bk​l|B_{kl}|_{1}=\tr\sqrt{{B_{kl}}^{\dagger}B_{kl}} is pk​pl​FBU​(ρ^k,ρ^l)\sqrt{p_{k}p_{l}}F_{\text{BU}}(\hat{\rho}_{k},\hat{\rho}_{l}). It therefore suffices to relate the Frobenius norms of the off-diagonal blocks of a positive semidefinite matrix to the L1L_{1} norms of the off-diagonal blocks of its square, via the following lemma.

Lemma 6.

Let

M=(ab†bc)\displaystyle M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b^{\dagger}\\ b&c\end{pmatrix} (43)

be positive semidefinite, with a,b,ca,b,c matrices. Write

M1/2=(xy†yz)\displaystyle M^{1/2}=\begin{pmatrix}x&y^{\dagger}\\ y&z\end{pmatrix} (44)

with the same block structure. Then |y|22≤|b|1|y|_{2}^{2}\leq|b|_{1}.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, assume that yy is non-negative diagonal. Otherwise, with a block-diagonal unitary

U=(u00v)\displaystyle U=\begin{pmatrix}u&0\\ 0&v\end{pmatrix} (45)

with uu and vv chosen to implement the singular value decomposition of yy , we may transform MM and M1/2M^{1/2} so that yy is a diagonal matrix with non-negative diagonal entries. For rectangular yy , the upper or left-hand square portion is diagonalized. This does not affect the norms, since UU transforms blocks independently and the L1L_{1} and Frobenius norms are both unitarily invariant. Let yiy_{i} be the diagonal entries of yy. Note that b=y​x+z​yb=yx+zy and |b|1≥tr⁡b|b|_{1}\geq\tr b, see Ref. [6], p. 432. Now tr⁡(y​x+z​y)=∑iyi​(xi​i+zi​i)\tr(yx+zy)=\sum_{i}y_{i}(x_{ii}+z_{ii}). By the positivity of M1/2M^{1/2}, yi2≤xi​i​zi​iy_{i}^{2}\leq x_{ii}z_{ii}, so yiy_{i} is less than at least one of xi​i,zi​ix_{ii},z_{ii}. Thus |y|22=∑iyi2≤tr⁡b≤|b|1|y|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{i}y_{i}^{2}\leq\tr b\leq|b|_{1}, as desired. ∎

Remark: Near the end of the above proof, because 2​yi=2​xi​i​zi​i≤xi​i+zi​i2y_{i}=2\sqrt{x_{ii}}\sqrt{z_{ii}}\leq x_{ii}+z_{ii}, the inequality yi2≤yi​(xi​i+zi​i)/2y_{i}^{2}\leq y_{i}(x_{ii}+z_{ii})/2 could have been used to obtain a stronger bound.

To complete the proof of Thm. 5, consider first the 2×22\times 2 block decomposition of R​ARA and BB with upper left-hand block (R​A)11(RA)_{11} and B11B_{11}. By Lem. 6, the squared Frobenius norm of the first block row and column excluding (R​A)11(RA)_{11} is upper bounded by the sum of the L1L_{1} norms of the corresponding block row and column in BB. By subadditivity of the norm, this is at most ∑i>1(|B1​i|1+|Bi​1|1)\sum_{i>1}\quantity(|B_{1i}|_{1}+|B_{i1}|_{1}). After a suitable permutation, the same argument applies to the row and column determined by Bi​iB_{ii}, for each ii. The proof of the theorem then follows by summing over the resulting inequalities and noting that each off-diagonal block occurs twice on both sides. ∎

VII Examples and applications

By a slight extension of an example already given, ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} is optimal when 𝒜\mathcal{A} is perfectly reversible on some code subspace and ρ\rho is a state with no support outside the code. Applications to reversing other simple quantum operations may be instructive. For instance, consider a qubit depolarizing channel 𝒜\mathcal{A} whose operator decomposition consists of (1−p)1/2​I(1-p)^{1/2}I and the (p/3)1/2​σi(p/3)^{1/2}\sigma_{i} for i=1,2,3i=1,2,3 with σi\sigma_{i} being the Pauli operators. For ρ=I/2\rho=I/2, ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} is the same depolarizing channel, whereas the optimal reversal is to do nothing. This case saturates the inequality of Thm. 5.

Due to its near optimality, the reversal operation ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} can be used in any situation where classical or quantum information has been corrupted by noise with known behavior. ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} has a simple definition, but whether it or a good approximation can be implemented efficiently depends on the details of the situation. Because its error is at most twice the optimum, it can be used as a theoretical tool to obtain upper bounds on the achievable fidelities in a given situation regardless of whether or not it can be efficiently implemented. The upper bounds can then be compared to the fidelity achieved by simpler algorithms. An example of this occurs in the use of stabilizer codes for quantum error-correction. When the noise model is independent and depolarizing, classical coding theory immediately suggests a combinatorially straightforward error-correction algorithm based on maximum likelihood error syndrome decoding. Comparing this method to ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} suggests itself as a fruitful path of investigation with applications to asymptotic bounds in quantum coding theory [12, 13]. More generally, for any encoding scheme capable of transmitting quantum information through a given channel at a given rate when appropriate decoding is used, ℛ𝒜,ρ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{A},\rho} may be used to provide such a decoding, with 𝒜\mathcal{A} taken to be the concatenation of encoding and noise.

Another application is to query complexity for quantum oracles. In this case, we are given a quantum black box implementing an unknown quantum operation from some set. A simple method for attempting to determine which operation we are given is to apply it to copies of some input state and attempt to distinguish the output state. A bound on the probability of success can then be obtained by using bounds such as the one of Thm. 5. This was how the fact that the hidden subgroup problem has low query complexity was first realized [14].
